description_full: Dynatrace, Inc. engages in the advancement of observability for digital businesses, which transforms the complexity of modern digital ecosystems in North America, Europe, the Middle East, Africa, the Asia Pacific, and Latin America. The company operates Dynatrace, an AI-powered observability platform, which provides solutions, including infrastructure, application, threat, and AI observability; digital experience; log analytics; application security; software delivery; and business analytics. It also offers implementation, consulting, and training services. The company markets its products through a combination of global direct sales team and a network of partners, including global system integrators (GSIs), cloud providers, resellers and technology alliance partners. It serves customers in various industries, including banking, financial services, government, insurance, retail and wholesale, transportation, and software. Dynatrace, Inc. was founded in 2005 and is headquartered in Boston, Massachusetts.
ceo_bio: Mr. Rick M. McConnell | CEO & Director | Age 59 | Compensation: $1.4M (FY2026)
culture_narrative: Employs approximately 5K people. Revenue per employee of $360K ranks in the below the sector median among Technology peers, improving at 24%/yr — growing workforce leverage. Each employee generates $95K of free cash flow annually. Stock-based compensation of $54K per employee reflects an ownership culture. CEO compensation is 4× revenue per employee (modest relative to workforce productivity). Governance score flags moderate compensation governance risk (4/10).
financial_summary: Dynatrace, Inc. is a large-cap technology business with a $12.5B market cap on $2.0B of annual revenue.

The top line has compounded at +20% over the past three years, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder. Operating margins are expanding by +7.3pp year-over-year, which is one of the strongest signals that the moat is deepening.
Returns on capital run at 9% against a 11% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests. Gross margins of 81% confirm genuine pricing power.

The business throws off $530M in free cash flow — roughly 26 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 3.45× so those profits are backed by real cash.
Accruals are elevated at -9.0% of assets, and Sloan showed firms building earnings through accruals rather than cash systematically underperform.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year.

Shareholder yield of 3.8% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and stock-based comp at 15% of revenue is silent dilution an owner has to account for, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.

sect: Its 12% operating margin runs 5pp above the Technology median (7%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It earns less of the sector's profit than its revenue share would suggest (0.52x).
Over five years it has been gaining share of the sector profit pool (+1.5% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 530 companies in the universe; the top four hold 29% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 33% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has pulled back 11% over the last three months.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 34% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 46% and a beta of 1.24, it amplifies market moves.
Liquidity is deep, with about $407.5M traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 47% in the 2020 crash and 49% in the 2022 bear market.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $22.35 (margin of safety -94%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 77%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $16.61 to $31.48 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Technology peers: P/E 80.4 vs 26.7 and EV/EBITDA 38.0 vs 16.4 (sector median).
Against its own history it is cheap: the EBIT multiple sits 62% below its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 4.2% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 2.0% (vs the 8% bar).
The 34 covering analysts target $64.26 on average, 48% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 9% falls short of the cost of capital of 10.9%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 1.53).
It runs a 81% gross margin and converts 26% of revenue into free cash flow, or 11% after stock compensation.
Earnings quality is mixed: cash conversion of 3.45x, but high accruals (-9.0% of assets).
ROE of 6% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.7x equity multiplier).
Operating margin is running 8pp above its own historical average, a peak-margin risk if conditions normalise.
It spends 23.5% of revenue on R&D and 14.8% on stock compensation (above the 2% gate).
hlth: The company holds more cash than debt.
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 5.1, in the safe zone).
growth: Revenue has compounded at 20.3% over 3 years and 23.5% over 5 years, so growth is decelerating.
At current returns, reinvesting 13% of profits supports about 1.2% a year of fundamental growth, too little to drive meaningful growth.
Free cash flow has compounded 20.7% a year over five years.
Forward indicators: a book-to-bill of 1.30 (orders outpacing sales), a backlog worth 1.7x annual revenue and deferred revenue up 14%.
Capex runs 1.7x depreciation (1.6% of sales), so it is building capacity for future growth.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.6%), and reported institutional holdings exceed 100% of shares (a sign of heavy share lending).
It returns 3.8% a year to shareholders (3.8% in buybacks).
people: With about 5,600 employees, each generates about $360K of revenue, in line with the Technology median, and productivity has risen 24.4% a year.
That works out to $95K of free cash flow per employee.
The company is founder-led, which often keeps management aligned with long-term owners.
CEO pay is $1.4M (4x revenue per employee).
